A French engineer who lives quietly in Paris has spent 30 years writing software that the entire internet now runs on without knowing his name. He wrote the code that streams every YouTube video, every Netflix show, every TikTok clip. He wrote the code that runs the virtual servers underneath AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. He calculated more digits of pi than anyone in history. He has no Twitter. He has no marketing. He just keeps shipping. His name is Fabrice Bellard. Here is the story, because almost nobody outside the systems programming world knows what one man has built. Fabrice was born in 1972 in Grenoble, France. He studied at École Polytechnique, the top French engineering school. He never went to Silicon Valley. He never built a startup empire. He just wrote code. In 2000 he started a project called FFmpeg, an open-source multimedia framework for encoding, decoding, and streaming video. He was 28. The project did one thing nobody else had done well. It handled every video and audio format that existed, in one library, on every operating system. He led it himself for years. Today FFmpeg is the invisible engine of the internet. YouTube uses it. Netflix uses it. VLC uses it. Chrome and Firefox use parts of it. Every Android phone, every iPhone, every smart TV, every video editing tool you have ever touched runs FFmpeg somewhere underneath. If you have watched a video on a screen in the last 20 years, Fabrice's code processed it. He was not done. In 2003 he started QEMU, a machine emulator and virtualizer. He wrote it solo until version 0.7.1 in 2005. QEMU lets you run any operating system on any other operating system. It became the foundation of modern virtualization. KVM, the Linux kernel hypervisor, runs on top of QEMU. Every major cloud provider, AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, IBM Cloud, runs virtual machines on infrastructure built around it. The Quick Emulator is the most cited piece of cloud infrastructure code on Earth. He kept going. In 2001 he won the International Obfuscated C Code Contest with a small C compiler that grew into TCC, the Tiny C Compiler. TCC can compile and boot a Linux kernel from source in under 15 seconds. In 2004 he calculated the most digits of pi ever computed at the time, using a personal desktop computer and an algorithm he derived himself called Bellard's formula. In 2011 he wrote a complete PC emulator in pure JavaScript that runs Linux in your browser, a project called JSLinux that engineers still cannot believe is real. In 2019 he released QuickJS, a small but complete JavaScript engine that fits where V8 cannot. In 2021 he released NNCP, a neural network based lossless data compressor that immediately took the lead on the Large Text Compression Benchmark. Then he turned his attention to large language models. He built TextSynth Server, a web server with a REST API for running LLMs locally. He released ts_zip and ts_sms, compression utilities that use language models to compress text and short messages at ratios traditional algorithms cannot reach. He released TSAC, a very low bitrate audio compression system. In December 2025 he released Micro QuickJS, a new JavaScript engine for microcontrollers, separate from QuickJS, designed for environments with almost no memory. Fabrice co-founded a telecom company called Amarisoft in 2012, where he serves as CTO. Amarisoft builds 4G and 5G base station software used by carriers and labs around the world. He has been running it for over a decade while continuing to ship personal projects from his own home page at bellard dot org He has no Twitter. He has no Instagram. He gives almost no interviews. His personal website is a flat list of projects with no styling, no fonts, no marketing copy. Just titles and links. A quiet French engineer who never moved to Silicon Valley wrote the code that quietly runs the internet. He is still shipping.

New course on serving LLMs efficiently -- how do you serve models to many concurrent users at low latency and reasonable cost? This short course is built with @RedHat and taught by @cedricclyburn . Efficient LLM serving requires efficient memory management. A 70B-parameter model takes ~140 GB just to load the weights. On top of that, every active request needs its own chunk of GPU memory, the KV cache, to store the token context it has built up so far. In this course, you'll learn to reduce a model's memory footprint with quantization and serve it using vLLM, which handles many concurrent requests efficiently through smart memory management. Skills you'll gain: - Quantize a model and measure the accuracy tradeoff - Serve a model with vLLM and watch it handle concurrent requests efficiently - Benchmark your deployment and make informed tradeoffs between speed, cost, and accuracy Join and learn to serve LLMs efficiently: deeplearning.ai/courses/fast… Video

One of the new, buzzy jobs in Silicon Valley is the AI Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), an engineer who is embedded within a client organization to help customize solutions, such as building and tuning agentic workflows that suit the client’s particular needs. I’ve heard from people who are wondering anew about the FDE career path since OpenAI and Anthropic started building new teams to place FDEs within client organizations. The rise of FDEs for AI workloads is one way AI is creating new jobs (and why the jobpolcalypse narrative of upcoming job market collapse is false -- there will be many AI and non-AI jobs). However, I believe there will be far more AI Engineer jobs than FDEs, as I explain below. The FDE role was pioneered about two decades ago by Palantir, which sent engineers to government locations to work on secure, air-gapped networks. In addition to having good technical skills, FDEs need communication skills and sometimes business skills. For example, they may need to speak with clients to understand their needs, formulate a strategy to prioritize projects, explain complex technology, and respectfully push back if a client asks for something unrealistic. They’re enjoying a resurgence because of the amount of work involved in taking an off-the-shelf LLM and building it into a custom agentic workflow that fits particular business needs. However, I believe the number of AI Engineer jobs will be far larger. A company might accept a few FDEs to be embedded within its organization. But most companies will want far more of their own employees working on their projects. While my organizations do hire FDEs, we hire far more AI Engineers! Also, a common client concern is that it is hard to find vendor-neutral FDEs — they are, after all, there to deeply integrate a particular vendor’s product into a company. In this moment when it’s hard to predict which AI service will be the best one in a year’s time, optionality (the ability to pick whatever vendor turns out to fit best in the future) is very valuable. In contrast, letting FDEs tightly bind a company’s processes significantly reduces optionality. Right now, I see surging demand for AI Engineers who can build software applications using AI software components (like LLM prompting, agentic frameworks, evals, etc.) and effectively use AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, and OpenCode). As the AI Engineer role matures, I expect it to fragment into more specialized roles, like the generic Software Engineer role from decades ago fragmented into frontend, backend, mobile, data engineering, devops, and so on. What will be the future, specialized AI engineering roles? I don’t know. Perhaps there will be AI FDEs, LLMOps Engineers, Evals Engineers, AI Data Engineers, Harness Engineers, and other roles we don’t have names for yet. But for now, I see a lot of AI engineers who are generalists create a lot of value. Skilled AI Engineers are in very high demand! As our field continues to mature over the coming decade, I look forward to new specializations within AI Engineering that create even more job opportunities. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

5/ The big picture Benchmarks for language, code, images, and reasoning are now well established. CAD generation and editing require different evaluation criteria. CADGenBench is an attempt to make those criteria explicit, reproducible, and comparable across systems. Leaderboard: huggingface.co/spaces/Huggin… Code: github.com/huggingface/cadge…

4/ Why three metrics? The metrics are designed to capture different classes of errors. Shape similarity measures overall geometry. Interface match measures whether mating features are present in the correct location and size. Topology match measures whether the fundamental structure of the part is correct. None of these metrics can fully replace the others.

3/ Topology match Geometry is not the whole story. Two parts can look similar while differing in their fundamental topology: • 4 holes instead of 2 • 2 disconnected pieces instead of 1 • a missing enclosed cavity To measure this, we compare the Betti numbers of the generated and reference parts: • b₀ = number of connected components • b₁ = number of through-holes / handles • b₂ = number of enclosed cavities These quantities are independent of the CAD system used to create the model.

2/ Interface match Many CAD features exist to interface with other parts. We therefore evaluate mating features such as: • bolt holes • slots • bosses • pockets Each feature is represented as a region that should either remain empty (keep-out) or contain material (keep-in). This captures errors that may have little impact on overall shape similarity but would prevent a part from assembling correctly.

1/ Shape similarity The first question is whether the generated part has the correct overall geometry. We combine two complementary measures: • Surface Distance F1 → are the surfaces located where they should be? • Volume IoU → does the part occupy the same volume? Together, they measure agreement in both surface placement and occupied material.

highlights.text_fr: C'est une sortie très excitante - Claude Fable 5 est le même modèle sous-jacent que Mythos mais avec des protections supplémentaires. Les benchmarks sont excellents et c'est le SOTA sur tout avec une marge, mais j'ajouterais que * qualitativement * aussi, c'est un changement d'étape méritant une mise à niveau de version majeure (à mon avis du même ordre que Claude 4.5 en novembre), culminant surtout pour les longues sessions de résolution de problèmes sur des problèmes très difficiles. Vous pouvez lui confier des tâches beaucoup plus ambitieuses que d'habitude, le modèle 'comprend' et il fonce, et il n'a jamais été aussi tentant de ne plus regarder le code du tout (mais ne faites pas ça en production !). Le modèle a toujours des particularités que les gens rencontreront et les protections sont configurées pour être un peu trop réactives au lancement, ce qui, espérons-le, pourra être ajusté avec le temps. highlights.text_fr: Ça marche vraiment bien d'ailleurs, à la fin de votre requête demandez à votre LLM de "structurer votre réponse en HTML", puis visualisez le fichier généré dans votre navigateur. J'ai également eu du succès en demandant au LLM de présenter sa sortie sous forme de diapositives, etc. Plus généralement, à mon avis, l'audio est l'entrée préférée de l'humain pour les IA, mais la vision (images/animations/vidéo) est la sortie préférée de celles-ci. Environ un tiers de notre cerveau est un processeur massivement parallèle dédié à la vision, c'est l'autoroute à 10 voies de l'information vers le cerveau. À mesure que l'IA s'améliore, je pense que nous verrons une progression qui en tirera parti : 1) texte brut (difficile/fastidieux à lire) 2) markdown (gras, italique, titres, tableaux, un peu plus facile pour les yeux) <-- défaut actuel 3) HTML (toujours procédural avec du code sous-jacent, mais beaucoup plus de flexibilité sur les graphiques, la mise en page, même l'interactivité) <-- début mais formant un nouveau bon défaut ...4,5,6,... n) vidéos/simulations neuronales interactives À mon avis, l'extrapolation (bien que la technologie n'existe pas encore) aboutit à une sorte de vidéos interactives générées directement par un réseau neuronal de diffusion. De nombreuses questions ouvertes quant à la manière dont les artefacts "Software 1.0" exacts/procéduraux (par exemple, des simulations interactives) peuvent être entrelacés avec des artefacts neuronaux (grilles de diffusion), mais généralement quelque chose dans la direction du récent viral nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982…. Il y a aussi des améliorations nécessaires et en attente à l'entrée. Ni l'audio, ni le texte, ni la vidéo seuls ne suffisent, par exemple, je ressens le besoin de pointer/désigner des choses à l'écran, similaire à toutes les choses que vous feriez avec une personne physiquement à côté de vous et de votre écran d'ordinateur. TLDR La fusion mentale entrée/sortie entre les humains et les IA est en cours et il y a beaucoup de travail à faire et des progrès significatifs à réaliser, bien avant de sauter jusqu'aux interfaces cerveau-ordinateur de type Neuralink et tout ça. actu.text_fr: L'un des nouveaux emplois en vogue dans la Silicon Valley est celui d'Ingénieur Déployé par l'IA (FDE), un ingénieur intégré dans l'organisation cliente pour aider à personnaliser les solutions, comme la construction et l'ajustement de flux de travail agentiques adaptés aux besoins particuliers du client. J'ai entendu des personnes qui s'interrogent à nouveau sur le parcours de carrière des FDE depuis qu'OpenAI et Anthropic ont commencé à constituer de nouvelles équipes pour placer des FDE au sein des organisations clientes. L'essor des FDE pour les charges de travail IA est une façon dont l'IA crée de nouveaux emplois (et pourquoi le récit de l'apocalypse de l'emploi de l'effondrement imminent du marché du travail est faux - il y aura de nombreux emplois IA et non-IA). Cependant, je pense qu'il y aura beaucoup plus d'emplois d'Ingénieur IA que de FDE, comme je l'explique ci-dessous. Le rôle de FDE a été pionnier il y a environ deux décennies par Palantir, qui envoyait des ingénieurs dans des sites gouvernementaux pour travailler sur des réseaux sécurisés et isolés. En plus d'avoir de bonnes compétences techniques, les FDE ont besoin de compétences en communication et parfois en affaires. Par exemple, ils peuvent avoir besoin de parler avec les clients pour comprendre leurs besoins, formuler une stratégie pour prioriser les projets, expliquer une technologie complexe et refuser respectueusement si un client demande quelque chose de peu réaliste. Ils connaissent une résurgence en raison de la quantité de travail nécessaire pour prendre un LLM prêt à l'emploi et le transformer en un flux de travail agentique personnalisé adapté aux besoins spécifiques de l'entreprise. Cependant, je crois que le nombre d'emplois d'Ingénieur IA sera beaucoup plus important. Une entreprise pourrait accepter quelques FDE pour être intégrés dans son organisation. Mais la plupart des entreprises voudront que beaucoup plus de leurs propres employés travaillent sur leurs projets. Bien que mes organisations embauchent des FDE, nous embauchons beaucoup plus d'Ingénieurs IA ! De plus, une préoccupation courante des clients est qu'il est difficile de trouver des FDE neutres : ils sont, après tout, là pour intégrer profondément le produit d'un fournisseur particulier dans une entreprise. À ce stade où il est difficile de prédire quel service IA sera le meilleur dans un an, l'optionnalité (la capacité de choisir le fournisseur qui convient le mieux à l'avenir) est très précieuse. En revanche, laisser les FDE lier étroitement les processus d'une entreprise réduit considérablement l'optionnalité. Actuellement, je vois une demande croissante d'Ingénieurs IA capables de construire des applications logicielles utilisant des composants logiciels IA (comme le prompting LLM, les frameworks agentiques, les évaluations, etc.) et d'utiliser efficacement des agents de codage IA (comme Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI et OpenCode). À mesure que le rôle d'Ingénieur IA mûrit, je m'attends à ce qu'il se fragmente en rôles plus spécialisés, tout comme le rôle générique d'Ingénieur Logiciel d'il y a des décennies s'est fragmenté en frontend, backend, mobile, ingénierie de données, devops, etc. Quels seront les futurs rôles spécialisés en ingénierie IA ? Je ne sais pas. Il y aura peut-être des FDE IA, des Ingénieurs LLMOps, des Ingénieurs Évaluations, des Ingénieurs Données IA, des Ingénieurs Harness, et d'autres rôles dont nous n'avons pas encore le nom. Mais pour l'instant, je vois beaucoup d'ingénieurs IA généralistes créer beaucoup de valeur. Les Ingénieurs IA qualifiés sont très demandés ! Alors que notre domaine continue de mûrir au cours de la prochaine décennie, je suis impatient de voir de nouvelles spécialisations au sein de l'Ingénierie IA qui créeront encore plus d'opportunités d'emploi. [Texte original : La newsletter The Batch]
actu.text_original: One of the new, buzzy jobs in Silicon Valley is the AI Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), an engineer who is embedded within a client organization to help customize solutions, such as building and tuning agentic workflows that suit the client’s particular needs. I’ve heard from people who are wondering anew about the FDE career path since OpenAI and Anthropic started building new teams to place FDEs within client organizations. The rise of FDEs for AI workloads is one way AI is creating new jobs (and why the jobpolcalypse narrative of upcoming job market collapse is false -- there will be many AI and non-AI jobs). However, I believe there will be far more AI Engineer jobs than FDEs, as I explain below. The FDE role was pioneered about two decades ago by Palantir, which sent engineers to government locations to work on secure, air-gapped networks. In addition to having good technical skills, FDEs need communication skills and sometimes business skills. For example, they may need to speak with clients to understand their needs, formulate a strategy to prioritize projects, explain complex technology, and respectfully push back if a client asks for something unrealistic. They’re enjoying a resurgence because of the amount of work involved in taking an off-the-shelf LLM and building it into a custom agentic workflow that fits particular business needs. However, I believe the number of AI Engineer jobs will be far larger. A company might accept a few FDEs to be embedded within its organization. But most companies will want far more of their own employees working on their projects. While my organizations do hire FDEs, we hire far more AI Engineers! Also, a common client concern is that it is hard to find vendor-neutral FDEs — they are, after all, there to deeply integrate a particular vendor’s product into a company. In this moment when it’s hard to predict which AI service will be the best one in a year’s time, optionality (the ability to pick whatever vendor turns out to fit best in the future) is very valuable. In contrast, letting FDEs tightly bind a company’s processes significantly reduces optionality. Right now, I see surging demand for AI Engineers who can build software applications using AI software components (like LLM prompting, agentic frameworks, evals, etc.) and effectively use AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, and OpenCode). As the AI Engineer role matures, I expect it to fragment into more specialized roles, like the generic Software Engineer role from decades ago fragmented into frontend, backend, mobile, data engineering, devops, and so on. What will be the future, specialized AI engineering roles? I don’t know. Perhaps there will be AI FDEs, LLMOps Engineers, Evals Engineers, AI Data Engineers, Harness Engineers, and other roles we don’t have names for yet. But for now, I see a lot of AI engineers who are generalists create a lot of value. Skilled AI Engineers are in very high demand! As our field continues to mature over the coming decade, I look forward to new specializations within AI Engineering that create even more job opportunities. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]
actu.decryptage: Andrew Ng analyse l'émergence du rôle d'Ingénieur Déployé par l'IA (FDE) et d'Ingénieur IA, soulignant la création de nouveaux emplois grâce à l'IA et la distinction entre l'intégration de solutions spécifiques (FDE) et le développement général (Ingénieur IA).

idees.text_original: A French engineer who lives quietly in Paris has spent 30 years writing software that the entire internet now runs on without knowing his name. He wrote the code that streams every YouTube video, every Netflix show, every TikTok clip. He wrote the code that runs the virtual servers underneath AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. He calculated more digits of pi than anyone in history. He has no Twitter. He has no marketing. He just keeps shipping. His name is Fabrice Bellard. Here is the story, because almost nobody outside the systems programming world knows what one man has built. Fabrice was born in 1972 in Grenoble, France. He studied at École Polytechnique, the top French engineering school. He never went to Silicon Valley. He never built a startup empire. He just wrote code. In 2000 he started a project called FFmpeg, an open-source multimedia framework for encoding, decoding, and streaming video. He was 28. The project did one thing nobody else had done well. It handled every video and audio format that existed, in one library, on every operating system. He led it himself for years. Today FFmpeg is the invisible engine of the internet. YouTube uses it. Netflix uses it. VLC uses it. Chrome and Firefox use parts of it. Every Android phone, every iPhone, every smart TV, every video editing tool you have ever touched runs FFmpeg somewhere underneath. If you have watched a video on a screen in the last 20 years, Fabrice's code processed it. He was not done. In 2003 he started QEMU, a machine emulator and virtualizer. He wrote it solo until version 0.7.1 in 2005. QEMU lets you run any operating system on any other operating system. It became the foundation of modern virtualization. KVM, the Linux kernel hypervisor, runs on top of QEMU. Every major cloud provider, AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, IBM Cloud, runs virtual machines on infrastructure built around it. The Quick Emulator is the most cited piece of cloud infrastructure code on Earth. He kept going. In 2001 he won the International Obfuscated C Code Contest with a small C compiler that grew into TCC, the Tiny C Compiler. TCC can compile and boot a Linux kernel from source in under 15 seconds. In 2004 he calculated the most digits of pi ever computed at the time, using a personal desktop computer and an algorithm he derived himself called Bellard's formula. In 2011 he wrote a complete PC emulator in pure JavaScript that runs Linux in your browser, a project called JSLinux that engineers still cannot believe is real. In 2019 he released QuickJS, a small but complete JavaScript engine that fits where V8 cannot. In 2021 he released NNCP, a neural network based lossless data compressor that immediately took the lead on the Large Text Compression Benchmark. Then he turned his attention to large language models. He built TextSynth Server, a web server with a REST API for running LLMs locally. He released ts_zip and ts_sms, compression utilities that use language models to compress text and short messages at ratios traditional algorithms cannot reach. idees.text_fr: Harvard University vient de voter pour limiter le nombre de notes A décernées dans les cours de premier cycle à environ 20% de la classe. Je ne suis pas favorable à cela. Cela va profondément à l'encontre de la façon dont je crois que l'éducation devrait être. Nous devrions maintenir un niveau élevé, mais aussi travailler ardemment pour soutenir le succès de 100% des apprenants, plutôt qu'une fraction. L'administration de Harvard a pris cette mesure - contre l'avis d'une grande partie du corps étudiant - pour contrer l'inflation des notes. L'inflation des notes est réelle : de nombreuses universités ont décerné des notes A et B à une fraction de plus en plus importante d'étudiants, et cela a rendu les moyennes de points (GPA) moins utiles comme indicateurs des compétences des étudiants. En même temps, nous voulons que les étudiants réussissent. Le cœur de la question est le rôle des institutions éducatives. Notre objectif devrait-il être : - Aider les étudiants à réussir ? - Juger les étudiants ? Les deux ont de la valeur. Mais mon objectif lorsque je travaille dans l'éducation est presque entièrement d'aider les étudiants à réussir. Pour moi, il est clair que beaucoup de gens veulent apprendre, être autonomisés, acquérir des compétences qui leur permettent de faire de nouvelles choses ! C'est sur cela que nous nous concentrons chez DeepLearningAI. Cette philosophie est aussi la raison pour laquelle mes cours en ligne (depuis mes premiers cours en ligne de Stanford sur Coursera) permettaient un nombre illimité de nouvelles tentatives pour les devoirs notés. Je crois qu'il faut laisser - et même encourager - quelqu'un à refaire quelque chose jusqu'à ce qu'il réussisse. Ceci est contraire au fait de juger du fait qu'il n'a pas réussi la première fois. De plus, je veux que les devoirs soient conçus principalement pour aider les gens à pratiquer et à apprendre, plutôt que pour juger de leur niveau de compétence. C'est pourquoi je préfère créer des "Problèmes pratiques" et des "Laboratoires pratiques" - des questions qui, lorsque vous y réfléchissez, vous aident à pratiquer et à renforcer ce que vous savez. Contrairement aux "Problèmes d'évaluation" conçus principalement pour juger du niveau de compétence. Mais la décision de Harvard ne rendra-t-elle pas les GPA plus significatives et n'aidera-t-elle pas les employeurs potentiels à identifier les candidats solides ? Ayant embauché un grand nombre de personnes de Harvard et d'autres institutions, je peux dire avec confiance que la GPA n'est pas un signal important. Nous avons des processus de sélection et d'entretien qui donnent des moyens beaucoup plus précis de déterminer si quelqu'un est vraiment compétent. Je n'ai pas besoin d'un plus grand écart dans les scores de GPA des candidats pour savoir qui est vraiment bon ! Pour être clair, il y a aussi de la valeur dans l'évaluation. Même si les tests standardisés sont très détestés, des tests de haute qualité comme le SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. fournissent des mesures objectives de la capacité dans un domaine. Je constate que la plupart des gens veulent apprendre et réussir. Il y a aussi des gens qui veulent une évaluation rigoureuse (par exemple, pour postuler à des admissions scolaires), mais c'est un besoin moindre, et ce n'est pas mon objectif lorsque je crée des produits éducatifs. Harvard est souvent décrite comme une institution éducative "d'élite". Il y a deux façons d'être d'élite : Une option consiste à limiter les inscriptions, puis même parmi les étudiants admis, à limiter à 20% le nombre de personnes qui réussissent bien. Je préférerais suivre une autre voie : fixer un niveau élevé et enseigner des compétences de pointe et avant-gardistes, mais s'efforcer sans relâche d'aider tout le monde à réussir. De cette façon, l'élitisme n'est pas défini par l'exclusion des personnes, mais par l'aide apportée au plus grand nombre possible pour être excellents. [Texte original : La newsletter The Batch]
idees.text_original: Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

idees.text_fr: Dans les temps médiévaux, dans la course aux armements de dispositifs de torture de plus en plus démoniaques, un génie sadique a eu l'idée de la 'Little Ease'. La douleur est implacable et sans soulagement et infligée par son propre corps. Les prisonniers devenaient fous en quelques jours. Un séjour à la Little Ease était considéré comme encore plus cruel que la roue, le pouce et les autres machines macabres de la Tour de Londres. Un porc de reproduction passera toute sa vie dans une version de cette boîte. Ce sont des créatures sociales et nomades (plus intelligentes que les chiens) qui ne quitteront jamais ce corset d'acier. Elles ont été sélectionnées pour être plus grosses que ce que leur ossature peut supporter. Pourtant, nous les mettons dans des cellules si confinées qu'elles ne peuvent pas s'asseoir confortablement, et leurs tentatives pour le faire (par exemple, en glissant leurs membres dans des stalles adjacentes) entraînent systématiquement des fractures et des entorses. Elles ne peuvent pas transpirer, pourtant elles n'ont rien dans quoi se rouler pour se rafraîchir. Sauf leur propre fumier, dont (contrairement à l'idée fausse commune) elles sont tellement allergiques (grâce à leur fort odorat) que les nouvelles truies souffrent souvent de constipation pour éviter de salir l'espace où elles mangent et dorment. Voici comment l'écrivain Matthew Scully a décrit ce qu'il a vu dans une "grange de gestation" de Smithfield : > "Plaies, tumeurs, ulcères, poches de pus, lésions, kystes, ecchymoses, oreilles déchirées, pattes enflées partout. Hurlements, gémissements, morsures de queue, combats et autres "Vices", comme on les appelle dans l'industrie. Mastication frénétique sur les barreaux et les chaînes, mastication stéréotypée "vide" sur rien, fouilles stéréotypées et construction de nids avec de la paille imaginaire. Et "défaite sociale", beaucoup de cela, dans chaque troisième ou quatrième stalle un être complètement brisé que vous savez vivant seulement parce qu'il cligne des yeux et vous regarde... des créatures au-delà du pouvoir de la pitié pour aider ou de l'indifférence pour rendre plus misérables, mortes au monde sauf comme tas de chair dans lesquels la tige [d'insémination] peut être enfoncée encore et encore pour reproduire de la chair." — Le Save Our Bacon Act tente d'annuler les quelques protections étatiques dont nous disposons contre cette cruauté barbare - par exemple, la Prop 12 de Californie - qui interdisait la vente de porc provenant de cochons gardés en cages de gestation. idees.text_original: In medieval times, within the arms race of ever more demonic torture devices, some sadistic genius came up with the idea of the Little Ease. This was a prison cell built so small in every dimension that a grown man could not stand upright in it nor lie down at full length nor properly sit. The pain is relentless and without relief and inflicted by one's own body. Prisoners were known to go insane within a few days. A stay at the Little Ease was considered even more cruel than the rack, the thumbscrew, and the other ghoulish machinery of the Tower of London. A breeding pig will spend her whole life in a version of that box. These are social, roaming creatures (more intelligent than dogs) who will never leave this corset of steel. They have been selectively bred to be bigger than their frames can support. Yet we put them in cells so confined that they cannot comfortably sit, and their attempts to do so (for example, by sneaking their limbs into adjacent stalls) reliably lead to fractures and sprains. They cannot sweat, yet have nothing to roll around in to cool themselves off. Except their own manure, which (contrary to the common misconception) they are so averse to (thanks to their strong sense of smell) that new sows will often suffer from constipation to avoid soiling the space from which they eat and sleep. Here is how the writer Matthew Scully described what saw at one of Smithfield’s “gestation barn”: > “Sores, tumors, ulcers, pus pockets, lesions, cysts, bruises, torn ears, swollen legs everywhere. Roaring, groaning, tail biting, fighting, and other “Vices,” as they’re called in the industry. Frenzied chewing on bars and chains, stereotypical “vacuum” chewing on nothing at all, stereotypical rooting and nest building with imaginary straw. And “social defeat,” lots of it, in every third or fourth stall some completely broken being you know is alive only because she blinks and stares up at you … creatures beyond the power of pity to help or indifference to make more miserable, dead to the world except as heaps of flesh into which the [insemination] rod may be stuck once more and more flesh reproduced.” — The Save Our Bacon Act is trying to unroll the few state protections we have against this barbaric cruelty - for example California’s Prop 12 - which banned the sale of pork from pigs kept in gestation crates. It’s incredibly important we don’t end up with this sort of federal preemption. SOB will not only kill the most important animal welfare related laws in the US of the past decade, but more importantly, it will also restrict ALL future legislative progress (aka how the animal welfare movement has gotten its biggest wins). The Senate is currently deciding whether to add the SOB Act to the Farm Bill. With relatively little money now, we can discourage the most pivotal senators in the Ag committee from backing this amendment. Defeating this bill is even more important given the amount of philanthropic funding I expect to come online in the next year or two. It will plausibly be over 10x more expensive to repeal SOB than to prevent it from passing in the first place. All that money that could be spent transforming our society's relationship to mass animal suffering will instead have to be spent just getting us back to where we are right now. That's why money spent now fighting this bill (and I mean right NOW) is so effective. If you’re in a position to donate six figures, please DM me.

Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) This is a super exciting release - Claude Fable 5 is the same underlying model as Mythos but with added safeguards. The benchmarks are great and it's SOTA on everything by a margin but I'll add that *qualitatively* also, this is a major-version-bump-deserving step change forward (imo of the same order as Claude 4.5 was in November), peaking especially for long problem-solving sessions on very difficult problems. You can give it a lot more ambitious tasks than what you're used to, the model "gets it" and it will just go, and it's never felt this tempting to stop looking at the code at all (but don't do this in prod!). The model still has quirks that people will run into and the safeguards are configured to be a little too trigger happy for launch, which can hopefully be tuned over time. I feel a lot of things changing as working software increasingly comes out on a tap. The Jevon's paradox kicks in and I feel my own demand for software growing substantially. You can ask for anything - explainers, visualizers, dashboards, bespoke single-use apps (e.g. a full wandb that is hyper-specific just for your project), you can 10X your test suite, auto-optimize code, run giant research projects with custom HTML for the results, anything! idees.text_fr: (Pour être clair, *je* ne pense pas que nous devrions essayer de ralentir l'auto-amélioration récursive de l'IA - je pense que nous devrions l'ouvrir et la démocratiser autant que possible. Mon point est : si *vous* prétendez que nous devrions ralentir, et que vous avez le meilleur modèle, vous devriez vous assurer que votre organisation ne peut pas l'utiliser.)
idees.text_original: (To be clear, *I* don't think we should try to slow down recursive AI self improvement - I think we should open it up and democratize it as much as possible. My point is: if *you* claim we should slow down, and you have the best model, you should ensure your org can't use it.)
idees.decryptage: Jeremy Howard clarifie sa position : il prône la démocratisation de l'IA auto-améliorable, et non son ralentissement, et critique ceux qui prônent la prudence tout en utilisant eux-mêmes les modèles les plus avancés.

idees.text_fr: Anthropic a choisi l'option *opposée* au chemin sûr : ils se permettent, le laboratoire actuel le plus performant, d'utiliser leur meilleur modèle pour la recherche IA de pointe. Ils ont dit qu'ils saboteraient les autres qui essaient. Cela signifie que la frontière de l'IA progresse, et le déséquilibre de pouvoir augmente.
idees.text_original: Anthropic has chosen the *opposite* of the safe path: they are allowing themselves, the current top lab, to use their top model for frontier AI research. They've said they'll sabotage others who try. This means the AI frontier advances, & power imbalance increases.
idees.decryptage: Jeremy Howard critique la stratégie d'Anthropic, estimant qu'en utilisant leur IA la plus avancée pour la recherche interne sans la partager largement, ils augmentent le déséquilibre de pouvoir dans le domaine de l'IA au lieu de suivre un chemin plus 'sûr' et démocratique.

idees.text_fr: Cela a également l'avantage essentiel d'éviter un déséquilibre de pouvoir dangereux.
idees.text_original: It also has the critical benefit of avoiding a dangerous power imbalance.
idees.decryptage: Jeremy Howard évoque l'avantage d'une approche plus ouverte et démocratique de l'IA, qui permettrait d'éviter la concentration excessive de pouvoir entre quelques mains.

idees.text_fr: quelques pensées aléatoires sur l'IA : - pour le code, je suis passé de 80/20 claude/gpt à 80/20 gpt/claude en <3 mois. surpris par cela à vrai dire, et intéressé de voir où sera la répartition dans 3 mois supplémentaires. - claude surpasse toujours gpt pour les trucs d'agents non codants. codex ressemble à un ingénieur (ce qui est génial pour le codage !), tandis que claude ressemble toujours à un collègue polyvalent. gpt manque toujours de cette magie du collègue - je suis assez meh sur opus 4.7. mon expérience n'a pas été mauvaise, mais elle n'a certainement pas été bonne. stable si quoi que ce soit. - anthropic doit régler le problème du calcul. on le sent en tant qu'utilisateur. les vibrations sont toutes déséquilibrées à cause de cela. mes opinions ci-dessus sont probablement en aval de cela. c'est un problème. - anthropic labs continue d'être le dieu de la stratégie produit IA. la conception de claude est un autre succès. c'est fantastique. je ne sais pas pourquoi on n'en parle pas plus ? a+ - l'application mise à jour claude code est géniale. j'ai finalement quitté le terminal pour l'utiliser. très bien fait. - comment les gens dorment-ils ENCORE sur le sdk d'agent claude ? j'ai l'impression de devenir fou. - gpt 5.5 est incroyable. le niveau auquel je lui fais confiance pour l'ingénierie est incroyable. si je ne pouvais avoir qu'un seul modèle rn, ce serait celui-ci juste à cause du fort besoin pour le cas d'utilisation du codage. - l'équipe codex tue. l'application a été le standard d'or depuis la sortie de 5.3 (mais je crédite l'équipe de conducteur pour l'innovation UI que tout le monde utilise maintenant). bien que je pourrais faire avec un peu moins de coups agressifs passifs contre ant de la part de l'équipe codex. TARS, augmente la classe de 30%. c'est une longue course les gars haha - j'ai désinstallé cursor ce mois-ci et je suis de retour à vs code pour mon ide. composer ne peut pas suivre claude/gpt, et le produit semble un peu décousu. plutôt enthousiasmé par la chose xai cependant, parce que leur équipe est absolument empilée et je suis impatient de voir ce qu'ils pourraient faire avec ce calcul. codex et claude code sont t1, cursor est t2. j'adorerais que cet accord fasse passer xai/cursor à t1 pour un vrai trio là-bas. - gemini...? on dirait que ce sont maintenant 2-3 modèles où le modèle semble être une excellente sortie et ensuite personne ne l'utilise jamais ? Je suis haussier sur google/deepmind mais étrange que cela ne se soit pas traduit par une utilisation du produit sous quelque forme que ce soit. plutôt déçu quand même - aucun modèle open source n'a atteint le niveau opus 4.5. J'espérais que le nouveau deepseek y arriverait, mais non. de bons agents oss devront attendre quelques mois de plus on dirait…
idees.text_original: some random ai thoughts: - for code, i went from 80/20 claude/gpt to 80/20 gpt/claude in <3 months. surprised by this tbh, and interested to see where the split is at in another 3mo. - claude still mogs gpt for non-coding agent stuff. codex feels like an engineer (which is great for coding!), whereas claude still feels like a general purpose coworker. gpt still lacks that coworker magic - i’m pretty meh on opus 4.7. my experience hasn’t been *bad*, but it certainly hasn’t been good. sideways if anything. - anthropic has got to figure out the compute thing. you can feel it as a user. vibes are all out of whack bc of it. my opinions above are all likely downstream of this. it’s an issue. - anthropic labs continues to be the goat of ai product. claude design is another hit. it’s fantastic. idk why it’s not talked about more? a+ - updated claude code app is great. i finally switched out of the terminal for it. very well done. - how are people STILL sleeping on the claude agent sdk? i feel like i’m going insane. - gpt 5.5 is incredible. the level to which i trust it for engineering is amazing. if i could only have one model rn, it would be this one just bc of strong need for the coding use case. - codex team is killing it. app has been the gold standard since 5.3 release (buuut i credit conductor team for the ui innovation that everyone is using now). though i could do with a little less passive aggressive shots at ant from the codex team. TARS, dial up class by 30%. it’s a long race guys haha - i uninstalled cursor this month and am now back to vs code for my ide. composer just can’t hang with claude/gpt, and the product feels a bit all over the place. pretty stoked about the xai thing though, because their team is absolutely stacked and i’m excited to see what they might be able to do with that compute. codex and claude code are t1, cursor is t2. i would love if this deal got xai/cursor to t1 for a real trio there. - gemini…? seems like this is 2-3 models now where the model seems like a great release and then nobody ever uses it? i’m bullish google/deepmind but weird it hasn’t translated to product use in any form. kinda disappointed still - no open source models have hit the opus 4.5 level. was hopeful the new deepseek would get there, but nope. good oss agents will have to wait a few more months it would seem…
